The bass and drums are the **foundation**. If they agree, a band can lose everyone else
and still sound like a band. This page is about how they agree. How the examples work is
explained in [the first lesson](arrange-band.qmd).

## 1. The bass follows the kick

The kick drum and the bass are both low and both short at the start of a note. When they
land together they sound like one big instrument. When they land apart, the bottom of
the band sounds busy and blurred.

Below, the drums play the same pop backbeat throughout. Try each bass line against it.
Look at the bass staff and the kick drum (the lowest notes on the drum staff) and see
where they line up.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="strum" data-chart="C|G|Am|F" data-tempo="96" data-on="bass drums" data-staves="bass drums" data-choice-label="Bass line:" data-choices='[{"label":"Dotted: 1, and of 2, 3","opts":{"bassFeel":"dotted"}},{"label":"Roots on every beat","opts":{"bassFeel":"roots"}},{"label":"Root eighths","opts":{"bassFeel":"eighths"}},{"label":"Root and fifth","opts":{"bassFeel":"alt"}}]'></div>

The **dotted** line is the one the style was written with: the bass plays exactly where
the kick plays. The others still work, but they make a different song: roots on every
beat is plainer, eighths push harder, root and fifth sounds like country.

## 2. The drums choose the feel

Now keep the bass line and change the groove. Each one divides the beat differently or
puts the backbeat somewhere else.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="rock" data-chart="C|Am|F|G" data-tempo="100" data-on="bass drums" data-staves="bass drums" data-choice-label="Groove:" data-choices='[{"label":"Rock backbeat","opts":{"groove":"rock"}},{"label":"Half-time","opts":{"groove":"halftime"}},{"label":"Four on the floor","opts":{"groove":"dance"}},{"label":"Train beat","opts":{"groove":"train"}}]'></div>

**Half-time** moves the snare from 2 and 4 to 3 only: the chords go by just as fast but
the song feels half as fast. Arrangers use it for a breakdown or a big final chorus.
**Four on the floor** puts the kick on every beat, which is why the root-eighths bass now
sounds like it's doubling something.

## 3. Swing: the bass walks, the ride keeps time

In jazz the roles change. The ride cymbal carries the time, the kick drum mostly keeps
out of the way, and the bass plays a note on every beat. That's a **walking** line: the
root on beat 1, other notes of the chord and scale in between, and a note on beat 4 that
leads into the next chord.

Compare it with the lighter **two-feel** (half notes) that a band often plays on the
melody before walking for the solos, and with plain chord tones.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="swing" data-chart="Dm7|G7|Cmaj7|Cmaj7|Fmaj7|Bm7b5 E7|Am7|Am7" data-tempo="140" data-on="bass drums" data-staves="bass drums" data-choice-label="Bass line:" data-choices='[{"label":"Walking","opts":{"bassFeel":"walk"}},{"label":"Two-feel","opts":{"bassFeel":"two"}},{"label":"Chord tones","opts":{"bassFeel":"arp"}}]'></div>

## 4. Latin: the bass anticipates

In son montuno and salsa, the bass plays the **tumbao**: it doesn't land on beat 1 at all.
The new chord's root arrives early, on the *and* of 2 and on 4, and rings over the
barline. The clave and congas mark the beat instead.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="montuno" data-chart="C|F|G7|C" data-tempo="104" data-on="bass drums congas" data-staves="bass drums"></div>

Switch the congas off, then the drums. With only the bass left, you can hear that it is
always a beat ahead of the chord chart.

## 5. Try it

- In section 1, play the **Root eighths** line, then switch the drums to **Half-time**
  in section 2. Which bass line would you choose for a half-time chorus?
